title: Thanksgiving Dinner: Will It Cost More This Year? It Depends Who You Ask
summary: If your family is cooking Thanksgiving dinner this year, the grocery bill might be a surprise. Grocery costs have risen nearly 22 percent over the past five years, according to federal data. Wars in Ukraine and Iran, tariffs from the Trump administration and severe weather around the world have pushed food prices up. Still, experts say it is unclear whether your Thanksgiving meal will cost more than last year's, or by how much. Two groups came to different answers. The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving will be up more than 6 percent compared with last year, with staples like cranberries and dinner rolls pushing the total higher. The Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute found something different. It says drinks like sparkling water and wine have become more expensive, but the average Thanksgiving food bill will come in a little cheaper than last year, thanks in part to sales and promotions. Wells Fargo chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson warned that a cheap turkey is not the whole story. Shoppers can still overspend on the rest of the cart, he said. Money worries are already changing how some families celebrate. In a recent survey by the website LendingTree, 53 percent of people said inflation was affecting their holiday plans or spending. Some are changing food choices, using coupons more or cutting back on guests. The survey also found that 51 percent expect to have company over, down from 59 percent last year. Philadelphia resident Andre Andrews, who is retired, said prices are 'too high.' He still plans to smoke a turkey and a roast for the holiday, even though they cost him more than before. LendingTree's Matt Schulz suggested sticking to a budget, shopping around for the best price and trimming the menu.
why_it_matters: Food prices shape what families can afford to put on the holiday table, so rising costs can change how people celebrate and who they can invite.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a big American holiday meal, and many families cook a large dinner at home with turkey and side dishes.
Each year, farm and food groups work out what that dinner costs by adding up the prices of the usual foods in shops.
Food prices can rise when wars, tariffs, or bad weather make it harder or more expensive to grow and move food.
Because prices change from shop to shop and sales can cut the bill, different groups can reach different answers about whether the meal costs more than last year.
